name: Airbus on AI in aviation, from autonomous flight to the factory floor
title: Airbus on AI in aviation, from autonomous flight to the factory floor
answer: Airbus's own site sets out how it applies artificial intelligence across aviation, from computer vision that lets aircraft take off, land and detect obstacles autonomously to the Skywise platform that analyses data across the industry. Its most concrete evidence is the 2023 Auto'Mate flight test, in which AI and cooperative control algorithms guided four drones to within 150 feet of a tanker aircraft without human interaction.

sections.body: This is the manufacturer Airbus describing its own artificial intelligence work on airbus.com, across an overview page on AI, a page on autonomous flight, and press releases from 2021 and 2023. The material is corporate and undated except where the releases carry dates, and it covers civil and defence aviation, helicopters, unmanned vehicles, space and factory operations. It is published by Airbus about Airbus, so it presents the company's programmes rather than independent assessment.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: Airbus frames artificial intelligence as a ubiquitous future technology and a key competitive advantage that lets it capitalise on the value of its data for customers, with ethical and legal considerations placed at the core of its AI activities. Its stated applications include transforming images and video into objects and activities through deep-learning detection and decision-making, and computer vision and machine learning that enable self-piloted commercial aircraft to take off, land, navigate and detect ground obstacles autonomously. AI also filters, classifies and merges mission-critical information exchanged by unmanned aerial vehicles sharing airspace, and a European defence programme connects next-generation fighters to other aerial vehicles through a system of systems enabled by advanced analytics and AI. On the ground, a Factory of the Future project aims to standardise software AI tools used for enterprise resource planning, and the Skywise open data platform uses AI to analyse disparate data sources across the aviation industry. Airbus also describes an AI-based robotic assistant for astronauts aboard the International Space Station and the use of satellite and drone imagery in an AI environment for catastrophe response and damage assessment. Its autonomous flight work spans an air-to-air refuelling demonstrator, autonomous features on the helicopter Flightlab, Extended Minimum Crew Operations, an Acubed project building certifiable autonomy systems, automatic taxiing trials, and a Vision Landing Application that analyses runway features in real time from onboard cameras.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The 2023 press release states that during almost six hours of flight test, four successively launched receiver drones were controlled and commanded using artificial intelligence and cooperative control algorithms without human interaction, guided to a minimum distance of 150 feet from the tanker, with a second campaign planned for late 2023 using AI-based navigation sensors. The 2021 release says the Vertex project on the helicopter Flightlab planned a complete demonstration for 2023. The overview page cites no figures.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For a reader following AI in transportation, this is a primary account of how a large aviation manufacturer is deploying the technology across flight control, maintenance-relevant data platforms and manufacturing. The Auto'Mate release is the most useful single item, because it reports a dated, quantified flight test in which AI guided multiple aircraft in formation without human interaction, and names the sensor work planned next. The overview and autonomous flight pages show the breadth of applications Airbus claims, from cockpit vision systems to factory software standardisation, which helps a reader map where AI is being tested in aviation beyond the cockpit.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Transportation

sections.body: The material is Airbus's own account of its programmes, so it is promotional in origin and gives no independent verification, cost, failure or certification detail. Several pages are undated overviews, and the two press releases describe campaigns that were planned for completion after publication, so the outcomes are not reported here. The site does not cover other manufacturers, regulators or the wider transportation sector.
